comments.capsule: Christ gives apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers, each by the measure of his gift, to equip the saints so that the body of Christ may be built from living stones.
comments.comment:
…These too he adds in sequence with what precedes. For if Christ is over all and through all and in all, yet to each of the saints grace was given according to the measure of Christ’s gift, so that some are apostles, some prophets, others evangelists, and after these pastors and, over all, teachers.

If then to be a teacher is a gift given according to the measure of Christ’s gift, clearly also a pastor who shepherds with knowledge must shepherd having a gift. And how will someone be an evangelist whose feet of the soul are not, so to speak, beautiful? And that they may become so, God must supply them beauty. But also a prophet who convicts and examines the unbeliever (for such is the prophet of the new covenant) must be thought appointed to the church from God. And if these can always be in the church, perhaps also apostles, to whom the signs of an apostle are given to work, can be found even now. There is need of apostles and prophets and the rest for the equipping of the saints, that they may be equipped according to the work of Christ’s ministry, so that the body of Christ may be built and energized from living stones.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the church has these different gifts and what they are for.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: One must aim at the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, put away infancy and every wind of teaching, and grow into Christ by speaking truth in love, as a body uses a head.
comments.comment:
…Yet one must make it one’s aim to arrive at the unity of the faith; and besides the unity of the faith, to come also into the unity of the knowledge of the Son of God.

When these have come about, putting away all infancy we shall be styled perfect men, having fully taken the measure of the stature that is in secret—which measure of stature is a measure of Christ’s fullness, all who have reached the said stature’s measure having held Christ’s fullness—when they will no longer be infants, nor because of being unmoored and doubtful about dogmas walk in an infant’s condition about them, as if carried about by a surge of the persuasive points for each falsehood and giving themselves to every wind of teaching: some people not disposed toward lying but teaching by dice-play, others deceiving with all craft and cleverness, because error uses countless methods against us.

And when the saints arrive at the said perfect man, then by having understood love, speaking truth in it, they will grow into Christ all the truth-seeds given them, using Christ as a body uses a head.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means by perfect men and by being tossed about by every wind of teaching.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul’s “that we may no longer be infants” can be read as modesty on his part, or as meaning that next to the ends laid up for the saints he was still an infant.
comments.comment: Since he says “that we may no longer be infants,” we ask whether he said this by moderation, including himself though not an infant, or whether seeing how far short the one who knows in part and prophesies in part falls of perfection he truly says he is an infant. The one who says he spoke by moderation will use “when I was a child, I spoke as a child, I thought as a child; when I became a man, I put away the things of the child.” The other will answer that by comparison with the many Paul had become a man, but toward the ends laid up for the saints he was still an infant; for the prophetic word names all “children,” saying, “Behold, I and the children God has given me.”
comments.selected_reason: Asks whether Paul counts himself among the infants, and gives both answers.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul may have been carried about by every wind of teaching as a man who saw strong arguments on both sides, like a ship wrestling with winds, yet not dragged down or shipwrecked.
comments.comment: After this you will mark whether Paul by moderation says not only that he is an infant, but also tossed and carried about by every wind of teaching and the rest. Yet the one who says even this was not spoken from moderation will say that as a man he was sharp and quick to hit, and saw arguments attempted on both sides sufficient to distract and put in a surge the one who contemplates the persuasions; and for that reason, as a man, he was carried about by every wind of teaching—not dragged down or shipwrecked, but like a ship wrestling with varied winds; and he saw the opponents’ arguments, as of people teaching in dice-play, not contemptible but spoken most craftily, enough to deceive; and he hoped sometime to obtain God’s help toward putting away every distraction and speaking truth without distraction and growing in love into Christ, whom he knew as his head and the head of the whole body of the church.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The wind that carries people off can be tribulation or a deceptive word, and it moves those whose minds are on earthly things.
comments.comment: Let them become like chaff before the face of the wind. Let them become worthless. This is also said in the first Psalm: 'Not so the ungodly, not so, but like the chaff which the wind drives from the face of the earth' (Psalm 1:4). Their worthlessness shows not so much of substance as of intention; for 'those who think on earthly things' (Philippians 3:19), having become entirely of the flesh and of the members, are chaff not having a sheaf, nor a stable seat. Thus a wind briefly moves them. And this wind is able to be either tribulation or a deceptive word. For thus some are carried away by 'every wind of doctrine' (Ephesians 4:14) …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The mind is in vanity when it is set on worldly cares or on false teaching, the understanding is darkened when confused, and we must avoid both lest we be alienated from God’s life.
comments.comment:
…when the mind is either toward the things of life, misusing its power on them, or toward certain dogmas shaped as true that are not true, it is in vanity; for every worldly care is vain, and all false words that pretend to be truth. And when the understanding, which is a rational discourse, is somewhat confused, neither seeing the nature of what is said nor able to follow the varied things said, then it might reasonably be said to be darkened.

So one must neither be in the mind’s vanity nor darkened in understanding, lest we be alienated from God’s life while ignorance is in us and hardness of heart.…
comments.selected_reason: Explains what “vanity of mind” and “darkened in understanding” mean.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: We must care for our mind and understanding so that the Word enlightens them, since those alienated from God’s life are alienated by causes in our own power, not by nature.
comments.comment:
Yet into all these there is danger of falling for everyone who is in the mind’s vanity and darkened in understanding; hence we must care for our mind and understanding, that the understanding may be enlightened, the darkness being loosed by the true light—which is the Word of God—and the mind, turned back from affection for vain things, may be led toward God through the word of Wisdom.

If indeed through ignorance and hardness of heart those alienated from God’s life are alienated from it by their mind having come into vanity and their understanding into darkness, they are alienated from that life not by nature but from causes arising from us out of what is in our power.
comments.selected_reason: Explains that being alienated from God’s life is not by nature but from causes in our power.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Vanity of mind is having a mind and not using it to contemplate realities but handing it over to Satan, who binds it.
comments.comment: Vanity is the madness about sights, the contemplation of things that do not even exist, and also the disordered imagination in the mind. Paul clarifies this when he says, “In the vanity of their mind, being darkened in understanding, alienated from the life of God” (Ephesians 4:17-18). See how it is called vanity of mind when someone has a mind and does not use it for the contemplation of realities, but hands it over to Satan who binds it.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Those with a bad conscience still feel pain and can be healed, but those past feeling no longer feel pain when they sin and give themselves up to licentiousness.
comments.comment: And if we want to understand “who having become past feeling gave themselves up to licentiousness,” let us compare those with a bad conscience, tormented by knowing something base in themselves, with those who with all license multiply their falls. The former have not yet become past feeling, but still feel pain; therefore it is possible, if they meet rational help, for them to be healed so as to live the time ahead blamelessly. The latter no longer feel pain when they sin; therefore, not resisting even a little and not practicing self-control, they gave themselves up to licentiousness for the work of every uncleanness in greed.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what “past feeling” means.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Uncleanness in greed is adultery, and in urging purity Paul says one defrauds his brother by taking a brother’s wife.
comments.comment:
And I think uncleanness in greed is adultery; for elsewhere he says this in the first to the Thessalonians, in which: “For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from sexual immorality; that each of you know how to possess his own vessel in holiness and honor, not in passion of desire like the nations that do not know God; that no one transgress and defraud his brother in the matter, because the Lord is an avenger concerning all these things, as we also foretold you and testified. For God did not call us to uncleanness but in holiness and honor. Therefore the one who rejects does not reject a human but God, who gives his Holy Spirit into you.”

And observe that, urging us toward purity, he says one defrauds his brother in the matter if someone takes a brother’s wife; yet the Lord is an avenger concerning all these who have been defrauded, whether brothers or also unbelievers.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: To learn Christ is to learn virtue, so one who has learned and heard him will not walk in vanity, and the truth is found in Jesus alone.
comments.comment:
…to learn Christ is the same as to learn virtue, and to hear him does not differ from understanding the word of the recorded conceptions of the Son of God. So if someone has learned Christ and heard him, since he learned him as Wisdom and heard him as God’s Word, receiving what he learned and heard, he will not walk in the vanity of his mind, nor be darkened in understanding, nor alienated from God’s life.

Let us therefore learn Christ and hear him; yet one must not despair also of being taught by a divine power that subjects to our purified mind a perfect and true word about Christ, as truth is in Jesus. He taught what learning Christ and hearing and being taught is by saying “as truth is in Jesus”; for the prototype substance of the truth is in Jesus alone, who says, “I am the truth.”
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to learn Christ.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Read in a different order, the verse means that as truth is in Jesus, so it will be in those who have learned Christ and put off the old man.
comments.comment: And “that you put off according to the former way of life the old man,” being disconnected, see whether we can restore it thus: but you did not so learn Christ, if indeed you heard him and were taught in him to put off according to the former way of life the old man being corrupted according to the desires of deceit, as truth is in Jesus—so that the sense is: as truth is in Jesus, so it will also be in you who have learned Christ and heard him and been taught in him, having put off according to the former way of life the old man being corrupted according to the desires of deceit.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The old man is constantly corrupted by a deceitful former life, but God kills him to make him alive and removes every wrinkle of age when he is put off.
comments.comment:
…For by his former way of life and the desires of deceit, through sinning and never doing anything that belongs to incorruption but working everything that belongs to corruption, this man is always being corrupted. So the desires of deceit and the former way of life bring about his corruption; and as long as he does these things he has not yet been wholly corrupted, but he is being corrupted. The Word of God, however, does not corrupt: he kills the old man in order to make him alive. “For I kill,” he says, “and I make alive” (Deuteronomy 32:39); and “when he killed them, then they sought him” (Psalm 78:34).

You will ask further how the old man is the one grown old in wickedness. Perhaps, just as virtue renews and creates afresh, so wickedness, its opposite, makes old, so that signs of age, wrinkles as it were, appear on the soul, as they do on bodies growing old. That is why Christ presents the church to himself glorious, “not having spot or wrinkle or any such thing” (Ephesians 5:27). For as long as one bears the signs of age, one has the wrinkle too; but when one puts off the old man, everything is in its prime and every wrinkle vanishes. And the desire of deceit is wicked and base desire.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what putting off the old man means in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Renewal in the spirit of the mind points to a spirit belonging to the mind that renews us once the mind is cleansed.
comments.comment: “And be renewed in the spirit of your mind” (Ephesians 4:23). If, by this wording, we must be renewed neither simply in the spirit nor in the mind, but in the spirit of our mind, we must ask on its own what our mind is and what its spirit is. Notice also the words “I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the mind also; I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the mind also” (1 Corinthians 14:15). Consider, then, whether, just as there are many spirits and each belongs closely to someone, so there is a spirit that belongs to our mind; and when our mind is being cleansed and has thrown off all its mist, this spirit, being its own, renews us.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Putting on the new man means showing Christ wholly formed in every action by imitating Paul as he imitates Christ.
comments.comment: “And put on the new man, created according to God” (Ephesians 4:24). If we want to put on the new man created according to God, let us take to heart “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Corinthians 11:1), and “I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). In a word, we will show Christ formed in us, whole, and in every action.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what putting on the new man means in practical terms.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The lie to be put away is false belief opposed to saving truth, and removing it requires testing everything and holding fast to what is good.
comments.comment: “Therefore, putting away the lie, speak truth each one with his neighbor” (Ephesians 4:25). Simpler readers will think that nothing more than a moral rule is said here. But we are persuaded that the lie is the opposite of the truth, and so the lie we seek to put away, the one opposed to the truth that is fittingly spoken to the neighbor alone, is false belief. It is no ordinary task to put away that lie, and to put away a lie of this kind; for one must be an approved money-changer, able to test everything, so that we hold fast only to what is good and keep away from every form of evil (1 Thessalonians 5:21–22). And what stands against the lie that lies in false beliefs is saving truth. The words “speak truth each one with his neighbor” are taken from Zechariah (Zechariah 8:16).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means by lie and truth in the verse.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: “Be angry” covers both an involuntary first stir that even the mature feel and a chosen assent to punish, and Paul commands putting away the assent.
comments.comment: “Be angry and do not sin” (Ephesians 4:26). It is clear that this is taken from the fourth Psalm (Psalm 4:4). The word “be angry” signifies two things. One is the involuntary, which some have called a pre-passion; it will happen even to the perfect, who suffer something involuntary when circumstances of this kind provoke them to anger. The other is when assent already accepts that it is fitting to punish the one thought to have done wrong; and this, since it lies in our power, the apostle commands us to put away. So it is the first of these meanings that is shown in “Be angry and do not sin,” in place of “even if you have at some time admitted anger, leave it without effect.”
comments.selected_reason: Explains the two senses of anger and what Paul commands.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Taking the command not to let the sun set on anger literally would be absurd.
comments.comment: “Do not let the sun go down on your provocation” (Ephesians 4:26). If we take this as said of the sun we see, then we will sin when we are angry and keep our anger while the sun goes down, which I think is absurd. …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The devil gains a place when the governing faculty lacks holy teaching and discernment, as Judas shows by yielding to the first prompting.
comments.comment: “And do not give place to the devil” (Ephesians 4:27). Origen says: this is like what is said in Ecclesiastes: “If the spirit of the ruler rises up against you, do not leave your place, for healing puts an end to great sins” (Ecclesiastes 10:4). We give place to the devil, or to the ruling spirit when it has risen up against us, whenever our governing faculty has not been filled with holy teachings, or with saving faith and with thoughts that discern and counsel us what is best. For, according to Zechariah the father of John, Satan settles on the regions of the soul; and such assents to what is worse, and leanings toward those assents, invite the devil to come into our souls. So too it is written of Judas the traitor: first, that the devil had already put it into the heart of Judas, son of Simon Iscariot, to betray him (John 13:2), and after this, that after the morsel Satan entered into him (John 13:27). So if, when the devil had put it into Judas’s heart to betray the Lord, Judas had stood against what was put there, Satan would not afterward have found a place to enter him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how giving place to the devil happens, with a clear example.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The devil turns away from the one who guards against giving him a place, but Judas, who did not guard himself, was entered whole by Satan.
comments.comment: The evil devil turns away from everyone guarding the command: 'Do not give place to the devil' (Eph 4:27). Judas, therefore, since he did not guard himself to provide a place for him, did not turn away from him, but rather, having first cast into his heart impious thoughts, Satan entered into him the whole of Judas and worked his evils, so that Judas would feel and know that the evil one was acting in concert with him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Even believers steal through dishonest trade under the excuse of need, while working what is good means earning an honest living to share.
comments.comment: “Let him who steals steal no longer; rather let him labor, working with his hands what is good, so that he may have something to share with one in need” (Ephesians 4:28). Many of those who are thought to have believed are busy with the affairs of life, and on the pretext of providing for their needs, even if they seem to be clean of idolatry and of all fornication, they do not easily keep from stealing when they buy and sell and do business with others. For this reason he did not hesitate to reproach them, as though some were still stealing (and this in Ephesus), as one who knew people of this kind. The very words “working what is good” point to an honest livelihood. Those who make their living unjustly work not what is good but what is evil; those who reverently secure what they need work what is good in this as well.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what stealing and working the good mean for ordinary work.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul wants us to give to the needy from our own labor as well as from our property.
comments.comment: …the Apostle urges us to share with those who have nothing not only from fields and revenues but also from the work of our hands. “Working,” he says, “the good with your hands, so that you may have something to share with the one in need” (Ephesians 4:28).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul wants labor to be used for.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: The good word builds up by teaching virtue and turning from vice, while the rotten word feeds vice and drives toward worse.
comments.comment: “Let no rotten word come out of your mouth, but whatever is good for building up as the need requires, so that it may give grace to those who hear” (Ephesians 4:29). Origen says: the good word, which builds up as the need requires and gives grace to those who hear, is the word that teaches, that urges toward virtue and draws away from vice. The rotten word is the one that feeds vice and stirs people up toward what is worse.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the difference between good and rotten speech.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Strictly the Holy Spirit forms no grieving judgment, yet our deeds grieve the Holy Spirit as far as it rests with us.
comments.comment: “And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” (Ephesians 4:30). Grief is a passion, and it is rightly defined as “a fresh opinion that evil is present, at which it is fitting to shrink.” But the Holy Spirit does not form opinions, nor (granting that it does) does it hold the opinion that evil is present to it. If that is so, the Holy Spirit will not be grieved. Is it, then, that as far as it rests with us, we grieve the Holy Spirit of God when we do these things? The Lord too says in Ezekiel, “And in all these things you grieved me” (Ezekiel 16:43). What we have often said about anger and wrath, about sleep and about words that speak of God in human feelings, is useful also for the discussion of “do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God.”
comments.selected_reason: Explains what grieving the Holy Spirit means.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Sealing imparts the Holy Spirit’s stamp while God remains undivided, to be kept unbroken until the day of redemption.
comments.comment: We were sealed with the Holy Spirit so that, receiving the stamp of the Holy Spirit while the one who sealed remains undivided, and taking the impressions of the Holy Spirit, we may become holy; and so that the spirit of the man that is in each of us may become holy, and, I think, the soul as well. The one who is sealed, then, is sealed with the Holy Spirit, but God is the one who seals. Everyone who, by believing God, has set his seal to this, that God is true (John 3:33), is sealed by the Father with the Holy Spirit; and he is sealed so that, by keeping the seal and showing it unbroken on the day of redemption, he may be counted among the redeemed.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the seal of the Holy Spirit is for.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Anger has been defined as desire to punish a supposed wrong, with bitterness ranked among its forms.
comments.comment: “Let all bitterness and wrath and anger and clamor and blasphemy be put away from you, with all malice” (Ephesians 4:31). Origen says: some have thought anger to be a generic passion, while placing it in turn under the genus of desire; and they have given this definition of anger: “Anger is a desire to punish one who seems to have done wrong improperly.” They list many species of anger, and among them they rank bitterness, as anger that is hard to receive or that bursts out at once …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Wrath begins anger in the soul and anger acts to punish, while bitterness is unsweet character and clamor is their noisy outcry to be put away.
comments.comment:
…Scripture seems in very many places to know a difference between wrath and anger, as in “Lord, do not rebuke me in your wrath, nor discipline me in your anger.” Yet we will not define in the same way the wrath of God that rebukes and the wrath that must be put away from us, nor the anger of the Lord that disciplines and our own. For what is said of God is said more figuratively, while what is named in us is, by common consent, passions and sins.

The word bitterness occurs also in Jeremiah: “And your bitterness,” he says, “has come up to me.” So I think the apostle is now speaking of bitterness in the sense in which we call some people bitter, the opposite of sweet; for common usage knows both sweet people and bitter ones. Wrath is the anger that is beginning to arise in the soul at something; and anger, perhaps, is not the genus of these and of others like them, but anger already ready and active for “the punishment of one thought to have done wrong.” And clamor, as a rule, follows these passions too: the bitter, the wrathful and the angry shout, and speak more noisily, and bring out words of bitterness, wrath and anger. So, in addition to the former, we must also train ourselves to have clamor put away from us.
comments.selected_reason: Explains wrath, anger, bitterness and clamor in plain terms.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Blasphemy to be put away includes angry speech against God, every slander of others, and calling true teaching false.
comments.comment:
The blasphemy here, which he commands to be put away from us, is, I think, what people often bring out from passion when they are angry, people who in the moment of anger dare to speak even against the divine; and blasphemy is again taken to cover every accusation against anyone at all, since those who speak ill of others are said to blaspheme those they speak ill of. So, following the words about bitterness and wrath and anger and clamor, it is said that blasphemy too must be put away.

If, however, we were also to class as blasphemy every utterance that speaks ill of the divine, not only when people speak evil out of grief and anger in times of displeasure, but often also from ignorance of the teaching of the truth, as is clear from the doctrines held among the heterodox, then the one who declares the true teaching false, or the false true, blasphemes too, above all about God and the things of God. Who, then, is so approved a money-changer as to know how to test everything, to hold fast to what is good and to keep away from every form of evil (1 Thessalonians 5:21–22)?
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Since Paul says “all,” no bitterness, wrath or anger remains permitted for any supposed good reason.
comments.comment: Some think that anger sometimes arises with good reason. They wrongly add to the gospel the words “without cause” in the saying “Whoever is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment” (Matthew 5:22); for some have read “whoever is angry with his brother without cause.” Let us put them to shame with the present text, which says, “Let all bitterness and wrath and anger and clamor and blasphemy be put away from you.” For here the word “all” is plainly said in common of them all, so that no bitterness is allowed, no wrath is permitted, and no anger comes upon us with good reason. And in Psalm 37, as though all anger were sin (and wrath likewise), it is said, “Cease from anger and forsake wrath” (Psalm 37:8). So it is never reasonable to be angry with anyone. And we must work hard to have put away from us not only all bitterness and all wrath and all anger and all blasphemy, but these together with all malice; and by malice we understand either the state opposed to virtue, or wickedness.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul says all anger must be put away.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Kindness replaces bitterness with approachable gentleness, and forgiving benefits ourselves even more as we imitate God giving in Christ.
comments.comment: “Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving yourselves, as God in Christ also forgave us” (Ephesians 4:32). Origen says: we named sweet as the opposite of bitter; but Paul seems now to call kindness what stands opposite bitterness, by a metaphor taken from foods. So we can understand “Be kind to one another” as meaning “people easy to approach, sweet and gentle in character.” This happens if we put away harshness, mercilessness and want of sympathy toward our neighbor and become tenderhearted toward all; and by this we give the greatest gifts not only to those near us but also to ourselves. For “forgiving yourselves” is something other than “forgiving one another,” since whatever good we do to others when we benefit them returns to ourselves, both because of its end and because we are of one body, more than to those we seem to have helped. And we give ourselves all that God also gave us in Christ, as it were receiving these gifts, keeping them, and imitating the Giver and his way of giving. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains kindness and forgiving in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God in Christ not only forgave our trespasses but also gave us wisdom, truth and righteousness.
comments.comment: … But how did God in Christ forgive us our sins? Is it because the Father, being in Christ, forgave us our trespasses? Yet in Christ he also gave us good things, if indeed in Christ is the wisdom that he gave us, and truth and righteousness.
comments.selected_reason: Explains forgiving as God in Christ forgave us.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Intercourse with a prostitute is fornication in Scripture's usage, while every other fleshly indulgence belongs to uncleanness, and shamefulness accompanies each form.
comments.comment:
“But fornication and all uncleanness or greed must not even be named among you, as is fitting for saints; nor shamefulness and foolish talk or jesting, which are not fitting, but rather thanksgiving” (Ephesians 5:3–4). … by the custom of Scripture, intercourse with a prostitute is called fornication; but every sin in the region of fleshly titillation, not only adulteries and the corruption of boys but also all the other things that human licentiousness has devised in varied and manifold rubbings, has been named, as a class, uncleanness.

… All uncleanness must be guarded against, since this is what is fitting for saints. There is a kind of shamefulness in each form of licentiousness; and in the same way shamefulness is also uncleanness, for every act in the region whose work is excretion shows both the unclean and the shameful. But this must be said of acts against nature, not of marriage.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means by fornication, uncleanness and shamefulness in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Foolish talk is the speech of buffoons and of all who are estranged from wisdom, jesting is laugh-raising of any kind, and saints are called instead to gracious speech.
comments.comment:
Let us see also what foolish talk is, which itself, too, must not even be named among the saints. Someone who takes the word more simply will say that foolish talk is what buffoons and jesters practice. But see whether we must not also say that all who are in any way estranged from wisdom and understanding talk foolishly, and that what they lay down as doctrine is foolish. The jesting that is joined to foolish talk will seem to agree with taking foolish talk more simply, for the usage of ordinary people applies the word to those who raise a laugh not only from foolish talk but from any cause at all. This too is not fitting for saints, but rather thanksgiving to God in all things, or else a “thanksgiving” that means grace, as when we call people gracious and charming.

So one must not be a foolish talker and a jester, but gracious and charming. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means by foolish talk and jesting and why thanks replaces them.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul threatens loss of the inheritance for fornication, uncleanness and greed alone, while foolish talk and jesting remain unfitting but less grave, and secret shamefulness holds back from the act.
comments.comment:
“For know this, that every fornicator or unclean or greedy person, who is an idolater, has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God” (Ephesians 5:5). We must observe that, having forbidden six sins (fornication, uncleanness, greed, shamefulness, foolish talk and jesting), he does not add of all six that whoever is guilty of any of them has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God, but of three, I mean fornication, all uncleanness and greed. For if the one guilty of foolish talk and jesting also had no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God, the judgment would seem to some rather harsh, since it would pardon our weak nature in nothing. These things are not fitting either, it is true; but not so that by doing them anyone falls from the inheritance of Christ and God.

It remains to consider shamefulness as well. You might think it reasonable to say, “every fornicator or unclean or greedy or shameful person has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God.” But perhaps shamefulness lies in the one who has been stained by passion only in secret, in which state a person, even when inflamed, has held back the impulse toward fornication or uncleanness. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul names only three sins as barring the inheritance.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The greedy person is an idolater because in loving money he worships the images stamped on coins.
comments.comment: Earlier we supposed that “greed” was put for adultery. So let us ask, from the words “or a greedy person, who is an idolater,” whether that reading is overturned or can still stand. Now we have found that in many places the prophets call idolatry fornication, as in “they went whoring after their idols.” And one could also take fornication to stand for idolatry, from the saying, “By a spirit of fornication they went astray” (Hosea 4:12). But if the greedy person is the one who gets money for himself from where he ought not, greed is called idolatry because those who love money are, as it were, worshipping the images engraved on the coins; for along with the coins these people love, as it were, the images stamped on them too. And I think the apostle somewhere also calls the love of money idolatry.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul calls the greedy person an idolater.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Empty words deny punishment for the wicked, yet God's wrath will certainly come, and the disobedient are called sons of disobedience as bearing their mother's likeness.
comments.comment: “Let no one deceive you with empty words, for because of this the wrath of God comes upon the sons of disobedience” (Ephesians 5:6). Origen says: He seems to call “empty words” the words that try, by some show of persuasion, to overturn the teaching about the punishments brought on those who have lived wickedly. At any rate he says that such words belong to deceit and are empty, because the wrath of God spoken of here will certainly come upon the sons of disobedience. He calls the disobedient “sons of disobedience,” as though the vice of disobedience became a mother and bore them, so that they carry, as it were, their mother's likeness. In the same way one can find in many places of the Scriptures “sons” and “children of fornication,” “sons of death,” “sons of Gehenna” and other phrases like these.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what empty words are and why Paul says sons of disobedience.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Partaker belongs to the better share in God and Christ, while fellow partaker here belongs to the worse share with the disobedient.
comments.comment: “Do not, then, become fellow partakers with them” (Ephesians 5:7). Note the words “partaker” and “fellow partaker.” Perhaps “partaker” is said of the better and “fellow partaker” of the worse. So, for example: “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your partakers” (Psalm 45:7), and, “For we have become partakers of Christ, if we hold the beginning of our confidence firm to the end” (Hebrews 3:14). I do not remember “fellow partaker” being used anywhere except in the present passage; but here it is clear that the fellow partaker belongs to the worse.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: What was once darkness can become light, so no one is doomed by nature, and those in the Lord walk as children of light.
comments.comment:
“For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians 5:8). If what was once darkness can change and become light, there are no natures doomed to perish. Just as the righteous are the light of the world, so the ungodly might be called darkness. The righteous, being light, will see light in light; but the unjust, being darkness, are a people sitting in darkness, seeing nothing. By their fruits we shall recognize who is light and who is darkness. For everyone who does evil hates the light, and, not coming to the light, he is darkness, a son of darkness and of night; but whoever does the truth comes to the light, and he is light, a son of light and of day (John 3:20-21). Besides this, consider whether “but now you are light in the Lord” is said of the righteous because there are some lights that are not in the Lord. It was especially fitting that the Ephesians, enlightened in the light of knowledge, should be told, “but now you are light in the Lord.”

“Walk as children of light” (Ephesians 5:8). If God is light and there is no darkness in him at all, then the children of God are children of light.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how darkness can become light and what walking as light means.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: A soul that receives the truth becomes light by faith and must also show it in works of light.
comments.comment: Therefore the soul having received the truth, the luminous word, and it itself is made light, and it hears from Paul: 'For you were once darkness, but now light in the Lord' (Ephesians 5:8). And when the intellect receives the evangelical light, it is named light according to faith; and likewise also according to works. For 'let your light shine' (Matt 5:16), he says, 'before men, so that they may see your good works, and may glorify your Father who is in the heavens.' For it is necessary for the one having received the light of faith to come even into works of light.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms that being light in the Lord means faith that shows in works.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Goodness does good, justice gives due desert, and truth knows reasons.
comments.comment: You will also bring them up short with the fact that Christ is justice. Goodness shows itself in doing good; justice in giving each what he deserves; and truth in knowing the reason of all things.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what goodness, justice and truth mean in the verse.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Goodness, justice and truth belong together in the light, so justice is with the good Father and not with another.
comments.comment: “For the fruit of the light is in all goodness and justice and truth” (Ephesians 5:9). These words are useful against those who separate the just from the good, and who think that the Creator is just, but that the one they imagine above him is the good God. For the fruit of the light is in goodness and in justice and in truth. Where there is goodness, then, there is justice; and where there is truth, there is justice. But goodness and truth are with the good Father; so justice too is with him and not with another.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Testing what pleases the Lord means examining each deed like a money changer and keeping what passes.
comments.comment: “Testing what is pleasing to the Lord” (Ephesians 5:10). We need to do everything with deliberation, so that, looking closely at each thing to be done and examining it, we may accept, like approved money changers, what passes the test and pleases God, and shake off what fails the test and displeases him. Since the phrasing is left hanging, it seems to me it could be restored like this: “Do not, then, become fellow partakers with them, testing what is pleasing to the Lord. Even if you were once darkness, now, being light in the Lord, walk as children of light, showing the fruits of the light in all goodness and justice and truth.”
comments.selected_reason: Explains what proving means with a memorable image a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Works of darkness are fruitless yet shared by their doers, exposing them belongs to the blameless, and their secret deeds of fornication and uncleanness are shameful even to speak of.
comments.comment:
“And take no part in the fruitless works of darkness” (Ephesians 5:11). Elsewhere too he gave the name “fruit” to what belongs to the Spirit and “work” to what belongs to the flesh, when he said, “Now the works of the flesh are plain: they are fornication” and the rest, “but the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace” and the rest (Galatians 5:19-22). Here, though, he says that the works of darkness are fruitless, and the one who does them takes part in them.

“But rather expose them” (Ephesians 5:11). Exposing, too, must be counted among the commandments. It will be done by the one who would not hear, “Hypocrite, first take the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother's eye” (Matthew 7:5). That is why the prophets, who were in no way open to reproof themselves, reproved those who sinned.

“For the things done by them in secret are shameful even to speak of” (Ephesians 5:12). By whom? He has not said quite clearly beforehand, unless one refers the phrase to the sons of disobedience, so that it reads: “For the things done in secret by the sons of disobedience are shameful even to speak of.” And those things were fornication and uncleanness.
comments.selected_reason: Explains fruitless works, exposing, and secret shame in plain terms.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Exposed works become light, the sleeper is roused by Spirit speech to repentance, and awake suits the spirit while rising suits the soul that sin kills.
comments.comment:
“But all things, when they are exposed by the light, are made plain; for everything that is made plain is light. Therefore it says, ‘Awake, sleeper, and rise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you’” (Ephesians 5:13-14). Origen says: Since the works of darkness, once exposed, are made plain by the light, as the things exposed are changed into light, it is said to those who are asleep and lie in deadness because they have done the fruitless works of darkness, “Awake, sleeper, and rise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.”

Someone might ask who it is that speaks in what is written here, “Therefore it says, Awake, sleeper, and rise from the dead.” One will say that the apostle read these words in one of the prophets and wrote them down here. Another will say that the apostle himself is giving a voice to words spoken by the Spirit, to urge people toward repentance.

You will ask, further, how the same person is told “Awake, sleeper,” as one who is alive and asleep, and “Rise from the dead,” as one who has died. Perhaps, then, it is this: there is the spirit of the man that is in him, which we have observed is spoken of as the better part; and there is something second, the soul, which can receive both sickness and death from sins. So “Awake, sleeper” is said because of the spirit, and “Rise from the dead” because of the soul; for “the soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezekiel 18:4), but nowhere have we found a death of the spirit. And Christ, being the true light, will shine on the one who is roused from sleep and has risen from the dead.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how exposure becomes light and why both awake and arise are said.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The sinner is dead, so Paul's call to awake and arise is a call back to the life of virtue that was before the fall.
comments.comment: A resurrection occurs both according to the soul and according to the body; 'Awake, sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine upon you' (Ephesians 5:14). Here, the one sinning is dead; for 'the soul, the one sinning, this one shall die' (Ezekiel 18:4); and: 'sin, having been completed, brings death' (James 1:15) to the one sinning. Therefore, awaken this one into the life that was before the fall; for this was the life with virtue. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Walking carefully comes from testing what pleases the Lord, and redeeming the time means buying it back from wickedness by spending it on what is needful.
comments.comment:
“See, then, that you walk carefully, not as unwise but as wise, redeeming the time, because the days are evil. Therefore do not become foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is” (Ephesians 5:15-17). Origen says: Whoever tests, in each thing he says and does and thinks, what is pleasing to the Lord will also be able, from close attention, to see carefully how he is to walk; and whoever sees carefully how he is to walk is wise in every way. And since some have a fairly good intention, yet, not being wise, want to see carefully how they walk, he added, “not as unwise but as wise.” For to see carefully, even in matters of conduct, is the work of wisdom.

“Redeeming the time, because the days are evil.” As if buying the time for yourselves, time that holds evil days as far as human life goes. When we spend the time on something needful, then, we have bought it and bought it back for ourselves, as though it had been sold to human wickedness. No one who lives too much for this life, caught up in cares or anxieties, has bought the time for himself; …
comments.selected_reason: Explains careful walking and redeeming the time in practical terms.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Redeeming time turns evil days into good days to come.
comments.comment: … And when we redeem the time that lies in evil days, we change the evil days, as it were, into good ones; for ourselves we make them, as it were, not evil days of the present age but good days of the age to come.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Do not become foolish but search out the Lord's will, doing it where seen and bearing what comes by it.
comments.comment: “Therefore do not become foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is” (Ephesians 5:17). “Therefore”: because of what? Is it that, because you are to look carefully how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, you must not become foolish? For if you are foolish, you will not walk carefully, nor as the wise do. He commands them to search out the will of the Lord and to understand it, so that wherever they grasp something about what they should do, they may do it as the Lord's will, and wherever they suffer, they may bear it as something that happens by the Lord's will.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what not being foolish and knowing the Lord's will look like.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Drunkenness with wine brings debauchery, and besides literal wine there is a wine of corrupt reasoning opposed to being filled with spirit.
comments.comment: “And do not get drunk with wine, in which is debauchery, but be filled in spirit” (Ephesians 5:18). Origen says: These words can be understood quite simply, since debauchery lies in drinking the wine that makes one drunk. But “wine, in which is debauchery,” can also be understood of the wine spoken of in the great Song: “Their wine is the rage of dragons, and the incurable rage of asps” (Deuteronomy 32:33). All who are out of their minds and drunk in their reasoning drink this wine, and it is full of debauchery. Set against that wine, which makes drunk and in which is debauchery, is its opposite: the one who has been filled with spirit and receives all of what is more divine that he has room for. We have often observed that the word “spirit,” written without any addition, is said of the better; and that is what it means here too.
comments.selected_reason: Explains both the plain warning and the second wine of wrong reasoning.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Hymns proclaim God's power, psalms order bodily conduct, and spiritual songs study creation, all sung sincerely to the Lord.
comments.comment: “Speaking to one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord” (Ephesians 5:19). Origen says: Hymns proclaim the power and divinity of God, and the one who has knowledge of how to speak of God would be in spiritual hymns. Perhaps the one who treats of what is to be done, and of the things one must carry out through our body as through an instrument, a kind of psaltery, is in spiritual psalms; and the one who, on the other hand, studies nature, the order of the world and the rest of what was made, is in spiritual songs. And we must sing in keeping with the study of nature, and make melody in keeping with the account of conduct, to the Lord, sincerely disposed toward what is said; for this is what it is to make melody and sing in the heart to the Lord.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what psalms, hymns and spiritual songs each cover.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Providence reaches all things, so thanks is owed always, even in hardships, in the name of Christ to God and the Father.
comments.comment: “Always giving thanks for all things in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to God and the Father” (Ephesians 5:20). In the First Letter to the Thessalonians, too, he says, “Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in everything” (1 Thessalonians 5:16-18). This commandment will be kept by the one who has understood that providence reaches even to the five sparrows sold for two pennies, not one of which falls into a snare without the Father in heaven. To give thanks in everything is also to give thanks for everything. So we must give thanks for hardships too, since these are also among the things for which we must give thanks. And just as a person in the world must give thanks for sharing in the world, for gazing at its beauty, and for seeing how many and what kind of things have come to be for the sake of the rational creature, so too we must give thanks for particular things. Whoever gives thanks to God and the Father must give thanks in the mediator between God and humankind, so that we do what is written: give thanks in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to God and the Father.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why thanks can be always and for all things.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Submitting to one another tears down love of ruling, following the apostles and the Savior who served, even when service looks like refusal for the other's good.
comments.comment:
“Submitting,” he says, “to one another in the fear of Christ” (Ephesians 5:21). This tears down entirely the love of ruling and of being first. For this commandment is given to all: “For though I am free from all, I made myself a slave to all, that I might win all” (1 Corinthians 9:19). And the commandment that says, “Serve one another,” orders the same (Galatians 5:13). That is why the apostles, through love, served the churches as slaves, ministering and serving the salvation of human beings. The Savior himself took the form of a slave, not so much for any other reason as to serve his disciples as a slave, so that once he even poured water into the basin and washed the disciples' feet (John 13:5). And the one who has understood, “Whoever wishes to be great among you shall be the slave of all,” submits by serving those whom he ought.

It is possible, however, for one who serves, and who in his service does what is suited to those he serves, to seem not to submit. This happens when those being served, not knowing what is good for them, order those who want to serve them to do things that are not suited to them. Yet even then the one who acts for their good both serves and submits to the need of the one he serves, because of the fear that, according to the word of God, is free of passion and makes us blessed. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains mutual submission through Christ and the apostles serving others.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Each marriage is to symbolize Christ and the church, the husband imitating Christ and the wife living holy as the church does.
comments.comment:
“Wives, be subject to your own husbands as to the Lord; for the husband is the head of the wife, as Christ also is the head of the church” (Ephesians 5:22-23). This saying wants every union of husband and wife to be a symbol of Christ and the church. The husband, if he orders the life of the marriage by reason, imitates Christ, the bridegroom of the church; the wife, if she lives with her husband as she should, strives to match the church's (if I may put it so) shared life with Christ. For so the husband will be the head of the wife, just as Christ is of the church. But if husband and wife are not joined to each other in this way, it could not be said of them that this man is the head of his wife as Christ also is of the church. So let each husband make it his ambition to be toward his wife as Christ is toward the church, and each wife toward her husband as the church is toward Christ. Let the husband think and do all that belongs to Christ, and the wife all that belongs to the church.

“But as the church is subject to Christ, so also wives to their husbands in everything” (Ephesians 5:24). Origen says: If wives must be subject to their husbands in the way the church is subject to Christ, then wives will have to live holy lives, free of passion and without sin, as they are subject to their husbands, just as the church is subject to Christ while living a holy life, free of passion and without sin.
comments.selected_reason: Explains marriage as a picture of Christ and the church in plain terms.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Spots and wrinkles of the soul mark sin and the old self, which only the Word removes to present the church holy.
comments.comment: “That he might present the church to himself in glory, having no spot or wrinkle or any such thing, but that it might be holy and blameless” (Ephesians 5:27). Spots are things like the freckles that form on the body, dark patches, white blotches and warts; once these are taken away, a woman would be more beautiful. Let us understand that corresponding things form on the soul too, and it belongs to no one but the Word to take them away, “that he might present to himself,” it says, his own bride, “having no spot or wrinkle or any such thing, but that she might be holy and blameless.” Wrinkles are a sign of old age. So if someone kept bearing traces of the old self and was not always being renewed, he might be said to be wrinkled in his soul.
comments.selected_reason: Explains spots and wrinkles as marks on the soul that Christ removes.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul's wording differs slightly from Genesis, as New Testament writers often do not cite the old Scripture exactly.
comments.comment: “For this a man shall leave father and mother, and the two shall become one flesh” (Ephesians 5:31). We should note, as we have done elsewhere, that the writers of the New Testament often do not set out the old Scripture in its exact words. On this point Genesis has: “For this reason a man shall leave his father and his mother and be joined to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh” (Genesis 2:24). But here, in place of “for this reason,” Paul has put “for this”; and he has left out the “his” that comes after “father” and the second “his” that comes after “mother,” as well as “and be joined to his wife.”
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Obedience can be read both as obeying parents who belong to the Lord and as obeying parents in accord with the Lord's will.
comments.comment:
"Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is just. 'Honor your father and mother'—which is the first commandment with a promise—'that it may be well with you, and you will live long on the earth'" (Ephesians 6:1-3). Origen says: The text is ambiguous. Either children must obey parents who are in the Lord, or children must obey their parents in the Lord. And neither reading should be rejected.

Parents in the Lord, as Paul was to the Corinthians, must be obeyed; and parents according to the flesh must be obeyed too, but in the Lord, when they command nothing contrary to the Lord's will. In either sense, obeying is just.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the two readings of in the Lord in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: By calling obedience to parents just, Paul answers those who separate a just God from a good God.
comments.comment: … At the same time, you will note this against the heterodox who separate a just God from a good one: to the disciples of the one they call "the good," he gives what they would call a command of the other God, if indeed that other God is the just one; and Paul says that it is just for children to obey their parents in the Lord, or to obey their parents in the Lord.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The second commandment also carries a promise, so first must mean either first legislation or first with its own proper promise.
comments.comment:
Some have read "which is the first commandment with a promise" (Ephesians 6:2) as if the commandments before it held no promise. For they think the first promise is set down on this one: "that it may go well with you, and that you may live long on the land which the Lord your God is giving you."

But these readers seem not to have noticed that a promise lies on the second commandment as well. "You shall not make for yourself an idol," it says, "nor a likeness of anything that is in heaven above, or on the earth beneath, or in the waters under the earth. You shall not bow down to them, nor serve them. For I am the Lord your God, a jealous God, repaying the sins of the fathers on the children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me, and showing mercy to thousands, to those who love me and keep my commandments" (Exodus 20:4-6). Observe that "showing mercy to thousands, to those who love me and keep my commandments" is a promise.

Perhaps, then, since the Ten Commandments were given to the people as their first legislation after they came out of Egypt, each of the ten commandments is a first commandment, spoken among the first of all that followed.

Yet someone who wants to hold to the plain sense of "which is the first commandment with a promise" will say this: the promise "that you may live long on the land which the Lord your God is giving you" belongs properly to the commandment "Honor your father and your mother"; but "showing mercy to thousands, to those who love me and keep my commandments" does not belong properly to "You shall not make for yourself an idol, nor any likeness."
comments.selected_reason: Explains what first with a promise means by comparing the two commandments.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul's quotation differs slightly from Exodus, raising how this fifth commandment can be called first.
comments.comment: … The text is taken from Exodus, which reads: "Honor your father and your mother, that it may be well with you, and that you may live long on the land which the Lord your God gives you" (Exodus 20:12). Here too, as he sets out the words, the apostle has left out the "your" after "mother"; in place of "and that you may live long" he has put "and you will live long"; and after "on the earth" he has left out "which the Lord your God gives you." Now this commandment is the fifth of the Ten Commandments. So we must ask how to take "which is the first commandment," when the first commandment given is, "You shall have no other gods besides me" (Exodus 20:3).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The promised long life points beyond literal land to the good land given after escape from spiritual bondage and endurance.
comments.comment:
Then again, the one who explains the whole Decalogue as made up of first commandments will object to this too. He will say that long life on the land which the Lord God gives to the saints is not given for the one commandment "Honor your father and your mother" alone, but for countless others as well. And such a person will need to gather the commandments to which "that you may live long on the land which the Lord your God is giving you" is attached.

After this we must inquire about the promise that grants long life on the land which the Lord God gives to the saints. We should not fail to see that the Jews think this comes about according to the letter. But we see that this is by no means true; the prophet too says, "Woe is me, that my sojourning has been prolonged" (Psalm 120:5). So we must look for the good land which the Lord God gives by promise to the one who has left the spiritual Egypt, who has traveled with all patience and endurance through the spiritual wilderness, great and terrible, and who has conquered the great kings whom the Lord strikes down and the mighty kings whom the Lord has slain.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the promise of long life as a spiritual land readers can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Masters must show servants the same sincerity, obedience to God, and goodwill required of servants.
comments.comment: "And you masters, do the same things to them" (Ephesians 6:9). Origen says: Which of the things said before are "the same things"? I think, then, that they are "in simplicity of heart," "doing the will of God," "from the soul," and "with goodwill" toward the household servants.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what do the same things means in plain terms.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Strength in the Lord means growing strong in wisdom, truth, and every aspect of Christ.
comments.comment:
"Finally, be strong in the Lord and in the might of his strength" (Ephesians 6:10). To be made strong in the Lord is to be made strong in the Word, in wisdom, in the contemplation of the truth, and in all the aspects of Christ. Of these the greatest is the might of his strength, mightier than virtue and its kinds, all of which are powers, just as the vices are powerlessness.

Among the virtues, as those skilled in these matters say, there is one that is not a matter of theory, called strength, so named because it bears some likeness to bodily strength; and another that is a matter of theory, called beauty, named from bodily beauty. It is with this beauty in view that we read, "Gird your sword upon your thigh, O mighty one, in your comeliness and your beauty" (Psalm 45:3); and in the Song of Songs, to the bride, "You are all beautiful, my companion, and there is no blemish in you" (Song of Solomon 4:7); and again in Psalm 45, "And the king will desire your beauty" (Psalm 45:11).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what being made strong in the Lord consists in.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God's whole armor is Christ himself, so putting on the armor means putting on Christ in all his aspects.
comments.comment:
… one can say that the whole armor of God is Christ, so that "Put on the whole armor of God" is the same as "Put on the Lord Jesus Christ" (Romans 13:14). For if the belt is truth and the breastplate is righteousness, and the Savior is the truth and the righteousness, it is clear that the Savior is the belt and the breastplate. In the same way he himself would be the readiness of the gospel of peace, and the shield of faith, and the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God: the Word who is living and active and sharper than any two-edged sword (Hebrews 4:12).

What other whole armor of God could one even imagine being meant, which the one who will stand against the schemes of the devil must put on, except virtue, which is Christ? For whoever has put him on, in all his aspects, will be able to stand against all the schemes of wickedness that are worked by its father, the devil.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the armor as Christ in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Ordinary fleshly temptation differs from the harder struggle when the enemy poses as a messenger of light.
comments.comment:
"For our wrestling is not against blood and flesh, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the world rulers of the darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places" (Ephesians 6:12). I think that wrestling against blood and flesh means what he calls elsewhere human temptations (1 Corinthians 10:13), when the flesh, desiring against the spirit, calls us to do its works. But it is no longer a human temptation, nor wrestling against blood and flesh, when Satan, disguising himself as an angel of light (2 Corinthians 11:14), strives to persuade us to heed him as an angel of light; or when something like this happens, which comes about with all power and signs and lying wonders, and with all the deceit of unrighteousness (2 Thessalonians 2:9-10).

And if the enemy should persuade someone to receive him as the Lord, who will say within him, "Thus says the Lord," so that the person even supposes he has become a prophet of the God of all things, the enemy would do this not as blood and flesh, nor as a human temptation, but as one wrestling with a man who has guarded himself up to that point. That is why no place at all must be given to the devil.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the two kinds of wrestling in plain terms.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: One reading holds that sins which seem to come from the flesh are first worked by hostile powers that stir desire, anger and hatred.
comments.comment:
Someone will say that "Our wrestling is not against blood and flesh, but against the rulers, against the authorities," and the rest, is said to teach us not to think that even the sins which seem to come to us from the mind of the flesh come to us first from flesh and blood, but from certain powers that work them. For there are demons that work love affairs and love potions, as the prophet also shows when he says, "They were led astray by a spirit of fornication" (Hosea 4:12). The same may be said of other demons that stir up rage and anger; by calling on them, the dabblers in magic are said to make a charm for holding down anger. And when we hate, we do not hate without the demons who work hatred; one could argue this, not unreasonably, from the so-called hate charms.

"Since, then, the apostle wants to teach us," he says, "that sinning does not come to us from the nature of the body, he says for this reason, 'Our wrestling is not against blood and flesh, but against the rulers, against the authorities,' and the rest." And as we ask what ancient Scriptures, revealed and made plain to him, Paul drew on in saying this, we conjecture that it came from the accounts of wars and single combats, such as David's fight against Goliath, and the fights of the sons of Israel against the foreigners or the nations they contended with and conquered. For it is likely that each of those is a symbol of spiritual rulers being defeated or prevailing. …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The struggle is against unseen rulers of darkness and wicked spirits dwelling in the surrounding air.
comments.comment: [Our wrestling] is, then, against authorities that are not visible or made of flesh; against world rulers of the darkness that surrounds the human race; and against the spirits of wickedness that dwell in the heavenly place, that is, the air. Elsewhere, at any rate, he said, "in which you once walked, according to the course of this world, according to the ruler of the authority of the air, the spirit now at work in the sons of disobedience" (Ephesians 2:2). For the air poured around us seems to be filled with opposing powers.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the rulers and spirits are in plain terms.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Withstanding the evil day requires the full armor, whether that day means this age or a contest still to come.
comments.comment: "So that you may be able to withstand," he says, "in the evil day" (Ephesians 6:13). Origen: Whoever seeks to withstand in the evil day must have the whole armor of God that the apostle set out. Because of it the opponent will be put to shame, having nothing bad to say about us (Titus 2:8): the devil, the accuser of our brothers (Revelation 12:10), who deceives sinners as his own, as men who have come to belong to his portion. Another will say that the present age is the evil day. A third interpretation, besides these two, will say that the struggle has no end for the one who has left this life: even the one who has conquered here will have to contend in another evil day against the opposing forces that appear.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the evil day may mean and why armor is needed.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Girding the waist means curbing the business of begetting to hasten toward immortality, and the breastplate of righteousness keeps one from rage and desire.
comments.comment:
"Stand, therefore, having girded your waist with truth" (Ephesians 6:14). In Luke too it is written, "Let your waists be girded" (Luke 12:35). We know what the belt is here: the one who has curbed the business of begetting, and no longer serves it but hastens toward immortality, girds his waist.

"And having put on the breastplate of righteousness" (Ephesians 6:14). The one who has put on a breastplate is harder to hurt when enemies shoot at him, and hardest to hurt in the vital parts. In the same way the one clothed with righteousness could not be wounded, not even like a deer struck by an arrow in the liver. For he will fall neither into rage nor into desire, but will remain pure in heart, because he has put on the breastplate of righteousness forged for him by God, the craftsman of all things, who makes the whole armor for each of the saints and gives it to him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the belt and breastplate in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Each piece of armor protects against a specific assault, from deceit and injustice to unbelief and false teaching.
comments.comment:
Insofar as someone has girded himself with truth, he will not be dragged into assenting to persuasive and sophistical arguments made on behalf of falsehood. Insofar as he has clothed himself with righteousness, he will be unwounded by the arrows of unrighteousness, since none of them gets through to make the one who has put on righteousness unrighteous.

And the one who has bound on the fine shoes of the readiness of the gospel of peace, being ready and having made his works ready for the departure, and having therefore become a man of peace, will neither do anything warlike or factious nor be condemned along with the unready. Unbelief, the enemy of the salvation of the human race, will have no room where the shield of faith is. And the one who has the helmet of salvation set about his head will keep unbroken the head of the soul, where the divine senses of the mind are. More than that, like a noble soldier, the one who holds the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of the Lord, will cut down and destroy every teaching that is at war with the truth.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Travelers need gospel readiness like Passover shoes, while those already perfected stand on holy ground.
comments.comment: "And having shod your feet with the readiness of the gospel of peace" (Ephesians 6:15). Observe that he has called a certain power of the soul "feet," with which, as it were, we travel, walking along the one who said, "I am the way" (John 14:6). These must be shod with the readiness of the gospel of peace. I think the shoes recorded in Exodus are symbols of these shoes, the ones that those who ate the Passover had to wear, being ready for the journey. For it says, "This is how you shall eat it: your waists girded, your shoes on your feet, and your staffs in your hands; and you shall eat it in haste. It is the Lord's Passover" (Exodus 12:11). Both eating in haste and eating with shoes on belong to readiness, so that, strengthened by the food, they might be able to travel. So let the one who is traveling be shod, and let the one who has reached the holy land take his shoes off. For it says, "Take off the shoe from your feet, for the place where you stand is holy ground" (Exodus 3:5). For this reason, let the one who is not an apostle have his feet shod with the readiness of the gospel of peace. But let the apostle no longer take shoes for the road, since he has already been made perfect and is in the place where, standing and walking, he is on holy ground, living in Christ.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the shoes through the Passover image a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Faith quenches evil thoughts before they can enter the heart, enabling the believer to stand firm.
comments.comment: "In all things taking up the shield of faith, with which you will be able to quench all the flaming arrows of the evil one" (Ephesians 6:16). Origen says: The arrows of the evil one are evil thoughts. So he will not be able even to begin to cast them into the heart when someone is covered by the shield of faith, since all the enemy's flaming arrows are quenched in it. And the one who carries the shield of faith will say, "In the Lord I have put my trust. How can you say to my soul, 'Flee to the mountains like a sparrow'? For look, the sinners have bent the bow; they have made ready arrows in the quiver, to shoot in the dark at the upright in heart" (Psalm 11:1-2). "Since I have put my trust in the Lord," he says, "how can you advise me not to stand up to the bows that sinners bend against me, and the arrows they make ready in quivers, wanting to wound the upright in heart? For look, I stand, and I do not move away, and all the flaming arrows of the evil one will be quenched any moment now."
comments.selected_reason: Explains the shield and arrows as faith against evil thoughts.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Spirit's sword is God's living word, working through constant prayer, watchfulness, and mutual help.
comments.comment:
… Sound speech flows from the divine Spirit, but its opposite speaks from the earth. For "the one who is from the earth is of the earth and speaks from the earth; the one who comes from heaven is above all, and what he has seen and heard, to that he bears witness" (John 3:31-32). The word that comes from the Spirit is a sword, and that is why Paul says here that the sword of the Spirit is the word of God. For "the word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword," and "piercing to the division of soul and spirit" (Hebrews 4:12), it cuts and divides.

It also does its work through prayer and petition for those who pray at every time, and who pray with the spirit, as in "I will pray with the spirit" (1 Corinthians 14:15). And it does its work for those who keep watch in order to grow rich in the word of God, and who persevere in acquiring it, so that they may both help others and, by their prayers, work on behalf of those who help them. Notice also the apostle's modesty: he asks the Ephesians to make petitions for him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the sword of the Spirit and its link to prayer.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Bold proclamation of the gospel belongs only to those whose hearts do not condemn them before God.
comments.comment: "So that speech may be given to me when I open my mouth, to make known with boldness the mystery of the gospel" (Ephesians 6:19). Origen: When the mouth is opened and speech has been given, then the mystery of the gospel is made known with boldness, and no longer in proverbs and parables. As the Savior too says, "The hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in proverbs, but will tell you plainly about the Father" (John 16:25). Only the one whose heart does not condemn him can take in the word spoken with boldness, and everyone whose heart does not condemn him can. For "if our heart does not condemn us, we have boldness before God, and whatever we ask we receive from him" (1 John 3:21-22). So the one who makes the mystery known with boldness is rare, because the one who has boldness before God is rare. "For who will boast that he has a pure heart? Or who will speak boldly, claiming to be clean from sins?" (Proverbs 20:9).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what bold speech requires in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul sends Tychicus to report his life as a pattern of good conduct and encouragement.
comments.comment: "So that you also may know my affairs, how I am doing, Tychicus, the beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord, will make everything known to you. I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that he may know how things are with you and may encourage your hearts" (Ephesians 6:21-22). Since the apostle's whole life, and every act and activity of his, came about by the Word of God, with Christ living in him, he sends Tychicus to report to the Ephesians the rule of his life and the order of his actions. And it was fitting for the apostle to send Tychicus for this very purpose, so that the Ephesians might have a pattern of good conduct. They were also going to be encouraged, as they learned that what was best, and what befits an apostle, was being achieved by Paul.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Peace is God's calming gift to the soul, and love with faith extends even to enemies.
comments.comment: "Peace to the brothers, and love with faith, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ" (Ephesians 6:23). Origen says: If there is any other gift given by God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ, peace is one as well. It is one of the most precious gifts, "the peace that surpasses all understanding," which "will guard the hearts" and thoughts of the saints (Philippians 4:7). It is a kind of calm and fair weather of the soul, a stranger to every storm, all unrest, and passion. Like peace, love with faith is also a gift given by God and the Lord Jesus Christ: love toward God, as it is written, "with the whole heart" and the rest, and toward one's neighbor "as oneself" (Matthew 22:37-39). Indeed, the one who has received love as a gift shows it even toward his enemies, hating no one and praying for those who mistreat him (Luke 6:28).
comments.selected_reason: Explains peace and love with faith as God's gifts.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Loving Christ in incorruption means abstaining from every sin that corrupts the soul.
comments.comment: "Grace be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ in incorruption" (Ephesians 6:24). Some have explained loving him in incorruption as being pure from the works of corruption, and the works of corruption are those of sexual union. That is why common usage calls those who are pure from intercourse "uncorrupted," and those who have tasted intercourse "corrupted." And some, stretching the point further, have taken "If anyone corrupts the temple of God, God will corrupt him" (1 Corinthians 3:17) in this way, though they cannot do the same justice to "But each has his own gift from God, one of one kind and one of another" (1 Corinthians 7:7). But see whether every sin may be a corruption of the soul, and complete abstinence from sin its incorruption. Then those who love our Lord Jesus Christ in incorruption would be those who abstain from every sin, and the grace of God is with all of them. As though there were some who love the Lord, but do not love him in incorruption, Paul says, "Grace be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ in incorruption."
comments.selected_reason: Explains incorruption as abstinence from all sin.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
